To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) folic acid is an effective targeting ligand for cancer therapies, (ii) folic acid can be exploited to carry an antigen to tumor cells to induce an immune response against the antigen, and (iii). folic acid can serve as a ligand to carry an antigen or a therapeutic agent to the tumor cells.
folate receptor-targeted immunotherapeutic agents can induce an immune response against cancer cells in vivo.
folic acid can be used as a targeting moiety to deliver haptens to tumor cells, thereby rendering the tumors more susceptible to attack by the host immune system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of folate-targeting strategies for the delivery of therapeutic agents to FR-positive tumor sites.

developing novel folate-targeted approaches to cancer therapy that exploit the natural biology of the folate receptor to deliver therapeutically useful molecules to the surfaces of FR-positive tumors.
the development of a new class of folate-targeting immunotherapies for the treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

folic acid is a useful ligand that has the potential to deliver a therapeutic agent to FR-positive cancer cells, but that the efficacy of the therapy is limited by the ability of the cancer cell to escape immune recognition.
folate-targeted therapy is a very promising and effective method for treating cancer.
folate-targeted tumor immunotherapy is a promising strategy to combat cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
folate-targeted hapten labeling of FR-positive tumor cell surfaces is a promising approach for cancer immunotherapy.

folate-targeted hapten therapy is effective against both established and newly formed tumors, that it does not cause systemic toxicity in mice, and that it is effective even in mice with a compromised immune system.
the folate-targeted delivery of haptens is a promising approach for cancer immunotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
folate-targeted hapten marking of tumor cells can induce potent antitumor immune responses in vivo and that the resulting immune responses can be harnessed to eradicate FR-positive cancers.
folate-targeted hapten marking of cancer cells is capable of stimulating the host immune system to attack and eliminate the folate-targeted tumor cells.
folate-targeted hapten labeling of cancer cells can be used to stimulate an antitumor immune response in vivo.
